Brake system failures do not always trigger warning lights or loud noises. In many cases, technicians identify issues only after slowing down, disassembling components and inspecting the system closely.

Understanding how brake system failures develop helps prevent more serious problems. Some failures remain hidden during routine checks and only become visible during a detailed inspection.

What brake problems can mimic ABS or hydraulic failures?

A vehicle may enter the shop with a rear wheel locking up during movement. This symptom often suggests hydraulic or electronic issues. Technicians may suspect a stuck parking brake, an ABS valve issue or a restricted brake hose.

However, brake system failures do not always involve pressure or electronics.

A visual inspection may show brake pads that appear serviceable. Once the caliper is removed, the condition may look very different. Pads may sit close to wear indicators. Friction material may be cracked or missing. In some cases, loose material can wedge between the caliper bracket and rotor, locking the wheel mechanically.

How does corrosion cause brake system failure?

Corrosion is a common root cause of brake system failures. It affects the backing plate, shims and pad contact surfaces over time.

As corrosion progresses, it weakens the bond between the friction material and the backing plate. When the bond fails, the material can delaminate or separate completely. This failure is difficult to detect during routine visual inspections.

Early signs often appear at the ends of the pads. Small chips or cracks may form. In other cases, the friction material may look intact but can separate under light pressure.

Thorough inspection is critical to identifying brake system failures. Technicians should not rely on a single-pad inspection. Both pads should be removed, measured and documented.

Corrosion should not be treated as cosmetic. It often indicates deeper structural issues within the braking system.

Wear patterns also provide important diagnostic clues. Excessive inner pad wear may indicate guide pin or caliper issues. Outer pad wear is less common and may signal binding or seized components. Tapered wear often points to hardware problems or restricted pad movement.

Brake system failures rarely result from a single cause. Careful inspection, attention to corrosion and analysis of wear patterns help prevent minor issues from becoming safety risks.

A hybrid vehicle is a different animal than many of us are used to seeing. After all, if the engine of a typical vehicle were to stall out at a traffic light, the driver of that vehicle would know something was wrong with it. If that same vehicle still drove with the engine off, then that would mean they were probably going down hill. But in the hybrid world, that is all normal. Several systems around the vehicle are impacted by two key elements: the engine does not run at all times; and the high voltage batteries need to be recharged on the drive.

The control side of a hybrid brake system contains differences, compared to its conventional cousins, to accommodate these conditions. All technical references here will be directed at 2005 to 2010 Ford Escape and Fusion Hybrid vehicles.

Regenerative Braking A hybrid vehicle recharges its high voltage battery through the use of regenerative braking. Energy can not be created or destroyed. It can only be transformed from one form to another. We all heard that one in science class, I’m sure. In the case of conventional friction brakes, energy of motion (kinetic energy) is being transformed into heat energy, via friction, and then dissipated into the air.

With regenerative braking, instead of just wasting that energy by releasing it into the air, it is placed in a box in the back of the car and saved as stored energy. Later, that stored energy will be converted back into kinetic energy that will pour back into the body of the car.

On a hybrid vehicle, the brake pedal acts as more of a human interface to the ABS module for a request for braking. Regenerative braking is the hy­brid’s first choice for braking. The ABS module “tells” the PCM or TCM (model year dependent) that a request for brakes has been made and how much braking is desired. The PCM or TCM then applies regenerative braking, via the traction motor inside the transmission, as needed.

More regenerative braking increases the amount of electrical charge generated for the HV battery at the same time it produces more drag to slow the vehicle down. During many light braking events, the rear friction brakes will be lightly applied and the front may not be applied at all until the vehicle is at a stop or near stop. For this reason, it is normal for a hybrid to wear the rear brake pads two and three times faster than the front pads.

For 2005 to 2009 models, the HV system is rated at 330V. 2010 models are now equipped with a more efficient traction motor that lowers the HV voltage requirements to 275V. For either system, you will notice bright orange wires that look like battery cables running throughout the vehicle. Those are the HV battery cables. Do not mess with those wires until you have been properly trained on that model vehicle. Simply put, those orange cables can kill you.

Electro-Hydraulic Brake Systems The 2005 to 2008 model Escape/Mariner Hybrids use an electro-hydraulic brake (EHB) system. The EHB master cylinder is also referred to as an actuation control unit (ACU). The bore of the ACU is called a pedal feel emulator and is primarily used to simulate normal brake pedal feel for the driver. The EHB system does not have a vacuum brake booster. The pressure generated for the calipers is not, under normal conditions, the direct result of the driver’s foot pedal efforts. The pedal generated pressure is normal only to stimulate a pressure sensor in the ACU that makes up the brake “request.”  Normally, the fluid pressure for the wheel hydraulics is generated by the pump and accumulator in the ABS HCU and is regulated by the teamed efforts of the ABS and PCM’s logic.

Under normal conditions, the driver’s pedal efforts are displaying to the ABS module as a “request” for braking. The ABS and PCM then divide the braking effects between the traction motor (for regenerative braking) and the friction brakes as needed.

“Normal” braking for this system typically means regenerative braking is providing most of the braking and the rear friction pads provide very little braking. The front may provide very little to no braking. Of course, at a stop or near stop the friction is applied to hold the vehicle from rolling.

The higher the request for braking, the ABS module and PCM electronically calculate and decide how to apply friction and regenerative braking to meet the demand. From feather-light braking to a panic stop, all brake applications are electronically calculated and delivered from a normally operating EHB system.

Only in the event that the ABS HCU can’t function to build pressure will the driver’s pedal pressure directly provide the hydraulic pressure for the calipers. There are valves inside the HCU that allow direct passage from the pedal feel emulator chamber of the ACU, through the HCU and to the wheels. This is called “manual mode.”

In manual mode, there will be no boost so the driver will have a very hard/stiff brake pedal. Braking efforts will be very high for the driver and will likely prompt them to tow the vehicle for fear of having no ability to stop at all. The complaints of “no brakes” or “barely stops” may be the common terms used by customers whose brake system has entered manual mode (failsafe mode).

The replacement of the friction material is the same as with a conventional system, however, the ABS module does test the brake hydraulic system’s integrity by pressurizing it during key-off events, such as opening the door or whenever the dome light is activated, and again when the key is switched on.

No one can predict when a brake line or hose will fail. This is why inspecting brake lines should be part of every vehicle inspection. Also, spotting and replacing a corroded line before it bursts can save the driver not only from an accident but also damage to the master cylinder and ABS modulator.

A brake line inspection checks the condition of a vehicle’s brake lines for leaks, corrosion, or damage that could affect braking performance.

OE brake lines are made from metal that is rolled and welded into tubing. To seal the tubing, molten copper alloy is poured into the line. On the outside, a coating or plating material is applied. In some cases, a plastic coating or paint is applied to increase corrosion and abrasion resistance.

Moisture and the depletion of the corrosion inhibitors in the fluid are the main sources of fluid breakdown. Corrosion causes the copper to be leeched from the tubing and deposited in the brake fluid. While it is rare for a brake line to fail completely from this type corrosion, it can lower the integrity of the metal shell over time.

The main killer of brake lines is abrasion. When the external coating is removed by road debris or rubbing on other components, the line will soon develop corrosion. The corrosion will spread and get under the coating. Soon, the integrity of the line will be compromised. This corrosion is hastened by road salt and deicers that become alkaline from reacting with the tubing.

Some automakers have changed the way they route and protect brake lines. It is not uncommon to see plastic covers over brake lines. Also, some manufacturers will minimize exposure of the lines by routing them in the wheel wells.

Materials are not changing. Steel is still the material of choice for OEMs. What has improved are the coatings used on brake lines, which are tougher against abrasion. Stainless steel is being used on some high-end vehicles, but it is very expensive.

Always pay attention to the position of the line that is exposed to road splash. This is the area of the line that will fail first due to abrasion.

Flaking or lifting of the outside coating is the first clue corrosion has set in. This is a clear sign the external coating has been breached and corrosion is starting on the lines.

Look at the lines that pass above the fuel tank. This area can become very corroded from the buildup of deicing brines and road salt that can’t be washed away. A rainstorm in July, for instance, could activate the compounds and cause winter corrosion in the middle of summer. A boroscope can help to inspect the lines in this area.

Document the condition of the lines. Taking pictures and making notes on the repair order can save you a trip to court. A few years ago, a manslaughter case was made against a mechanic because he did not tell the customer about corroded lines during a state inspection. Three months after the inspection, a leaking line caused a serious accident.

Inspect brackets and hold-downs. When a brake line is free to move, it can rub up against another line. As the vehicle shakes and vibrates, outer coating can be rubbed away.

Any sign of corrosion on a brake line is reason enough to bring it to the customer’s attention and recommend replacement, even if it is not leaking. If the customer refuses the repair, document it in the customer’s file. Don’t take chances.

Ever hear the saying, “The squeaky wheel gets the grease?” The saying actually refers to persistence and never giving up — not greasing the brakes.

Staying power is what special-purpose brake lubricants are supposed to have when the going gets hot. The front brakes on many FWD cars, as well as large SUVs, can get extremely hot when braking hard or braking repeatedly. Mountain driving, aggressive driving in stop-and-go traffic or off-road, towing a trailer, hauling a heavier than normal load, etc., can all increase the operating temperature of the brake system.

Under extreme driving conditions, some lubricants can’t stand the heat and melt off, evaporate, oxidize or burn. That’s why ordinary, general-purpose chassis grease should never be used for lubricating brake components. It won’t hold up. What’s needed is a specially formulated, high-temperature brake grease that can withstand the heat, and also not harm rubber seals or plastic bushings. Petroleum-based lubricants should never be used for brake assembly work because mineral oils can cause seals to swell and fail.

What needs to be lubricated? Mechanical components in the brake system that slide, move, rotate or bear pressure. Why do lubricants work to reduce some brake noises? It is a simple answer. When a caliper finger is lubricated at the point it touches the brake pad, the lubricant creates a boundary layer that separates the vibration of the brake pad from exciting the caliper finger and the caliper. This is one approach to solving NVH problems that can have its limitations. Lubricants do not dampen forces by adding extra mass like a brake shim. Also, lubricants cannot fill in pitting on brake slides. Additionally, lubricants do not insulate against vibration and is effective for some frequencies. The primary lubrication points in a drum brake include the raised pads on the backing plate that support the shoes, the star adjuster mechanism, hinge points for self-adjusters or the parking brake linkage, and the parking brake cables.

In disc brakes, lubrication points include the caliper slides and bushings, self-adjuster mechanisms on rear disc brakes with locking calipers, and the parking brake cables and linkage. Brake grease can also be used to dampen vibrations between disc brake pads and caliper pistons. But, it should not be applied between the pad and any noise suppression shims that may be used. Use it on the back of a bare pad or between the pad shim and caliper.

One place you never, ever want to get any grease on is the friction surface of a brake lining — which is another reason for not using low-temperature or petroleum-based lubricants which can melt, run off and foul the linings. Grease-contaminated shoes or pads will be grabby and usually cause a brake pull to one side. The only cure is to replace the fouled linings with new ones. Cleaning is out of the question because solvents and cleaners can adversely affect the linings, too.

When it comes to brake lubricants, grease is a dirty word. Brake lubricants are specially-formulated products that are not the same as ordinary chassis grease or even multi-purpose grease. The kind of grease that’s used to lube tie rod ends, ball joints and U-joints is not the same as the lubricants that are required for brake system components. In fact, ordinary grease may cause serious problems if it is used on brake hardware or hydraulic components.

As every technician should know, many petroleum-based products are not compatible with the seal materials that are commonly used inside brake systems. Petroleum-based grease or oil should never come into contact with the rubber seals, pistons or other internal parts in a master cylinder, brake caliper or wheel cylinder. If it does, the entire brake system should be considered contaminated. This will require draining and flushing the entire system, and replacing all the major hydraulic components! Why? Because petroleum-based products can cause incompatible seal materials to swell, rupture and leak – which could lead to fluid loss and brake failure.

Brake lubricants, by comparison, are specially formulated products that are designed exclusively for brake applications and nothing else. The chemicals in these products are compatible with all commonly used seal materials, and will not harm these parts.

Several Basic Types There are several basic types of brake lubricants: those that are designed for lubricating hardware and mechanical components and typically contain a high percentage of solids (dry film lubricants), and those that are designed for lubricating seals, boots and other internal parts when assembling calipers, wheel cylinders and master cylinders.

Brake lubricant for hardware is a special high temperature grease designed to provide long-lasting protection. The lubricant may be a synthetic or silicone-based product. Synthetic-based, boundary-type lubricants that come in a tube, paste or stick form have a high solids content and typically contain a variety of friction-reducing ingredients such as molybdenum disulfide (moly or MOS2) and graphite.

Moly and graphite are both dry-film lubricants that can handle high temperatures and pressures. Some of these products are rated to withstand intermittent temperatures as high as 2,400 degrees F!

Moly and graphite have excellent staying power and won’t evaporate or burn off over time, and they won’t attract or hold dirt like ordinary “wet” greases can. This type of product is ideal for high temperature applications where long-lasting metal-to-metal lubrication is essential for good brake performance.

AUMOVIO is unveiling its distributed brake system, the latest generation of its electrohydraulic brakes. The company said the system delivers greater performance in a compact design. A major Chinese vehicle manufacturer has placed the first order. AUMOVIO plans to start production at the end of 2027.

AUMOVIO Distributed Brake Combines Two Systems

The distributed brake combines an advanced one-box brake with an electronic stability control system. The system operates fully electronically from the brake pedal through the fallback level. It also uses modern electrical and electronic architectures. This approach allows engineers to design smaller and lighter actuators.

The system frees installation space for components such as larger high-voltage batteries. It also gives manufacturers more flexibility when placing actuators in the vehicle. AUMOVIO said the distributed brake delivers greater performance than previous one-box systems. This performance makes it suitable for demanding applications such as highly automated driving.

“The mobility of the future is automated, electric, and increasingly based on new vehicle architectures. This transformation will not happen overnight, but step by step. With our solutions ranging from electrohydraulic to fully dry braking systems, our customers can draw on a very broad product portfolio,” said Boris Mergell, head of the safety and motion business area at AUMOVIO. “The new distributed brake system expands this portfolio even further. It gives our customers even greater flexibility, efficiency, and powerful performance. With its first series order, our new system is taking an important step toward high-volume production.”

Intelligent Redundancy Keeps Both Actuators Active

Current one-box brake systems for highly automated driving contain two brake actuators. However, they use only one during normal operation. The second actuator serves as a fallback. By contrast, the distributed brake system keeps both brake actuators permanently active.

This design allows them to generate braking force together when required. Each braking system can function independently during a fallback. Manufacturers can therefore make distributed brake systems smaller, lighter and more energy-efficient than previous one-box systems.

AUMOVIO said it has increased braking performance by coordinating the actuators. The improvement applies during normal driving and emergency operation. Most other braking systems act on only two or three wheels in fallback mode. The distributed brake system continues to access all four wheels.

This capability supports highly automated driving, where safety during an electrical failure remains crucial. Distributed brake systems can support automated driving up to SAE Level 5.

Modern E/E Architectures Expand Vehicle Applications

AUMOVIO uses the electrical and electronic architecture of modern vehicles for the distributed brake system. This architecture includes multiple power supply points and redundant electrical networks. The architecture meets requirements for braking systems without a hydraulic fallback. These systems require a redundant system with its own electrical circuit.

The system transmits the driver’s braking commands electronically. It does not require a hydraulic fallback with a mechanical connection to the driver. Manufacturers can position almost all braking system components freely in the vehicle’s front section. The electronic brake pedal remains the exception.

This flexibility supports new vehicle concepts and improves the use of installation space. For example, manufacturers can install larger batteries to extend vehicle range. The distributed brake system works with many vehicle types. Fully electric and hybrid vehicles commonly use redundant electrical and electronic architectures. Many new combustion-engine vehicles also use these architectures.

The distributed brake system lacks a mechanical-hydraulic connection between the brake pedal and braking system. This design provides additional benefits. For example, engineers can increase the air gap between the brake disc and brake caliper. The system builds fallback brake pressure electronically with greater precision and speed. This design reduces unwanted friction between the brake disc and brake caliper.

A single e-pedal braking system can also work across a wide range of vehicle architectures. Manufacturers currently use slightly different variants for left- or right-hand-drive vehicles and different powertrains. Instead, manufacturers can equip these vehicles with the same e-pedal braking solution.

This approach reduces the number of variants. It can also lower development, manufacturing and logistics costs for suppliers and vehicle manufacturers.

Distributed Brake Expands Braking Portfolio

AUMOVIO noted that it draws on 120 years of experience in vehicle safety. Its recent braking developments include electrohydraulic pressure providers in MK C 1 and MK C 2 one-box systems. The company has sold more than 15 million of these systems since their 2016 market launch.

AUMOVIO has incorporated this experience into a brake-by-wire application. The design combines hydraulic brakes with an electromechanical brake architecture. The system aims to provide higher performance while using resources more efficiently. These resources include energy, installation space and costs throughout development, manufacturing and service life.

Long before streaming platforms, smartphones, and social media, audiences watched movies without a single spoken word. Silent films relied entirely on visuals to tell the story, and people followed along just fine. Visuals carried the message then, and they still do today.

In today’s automotive aftermarket, images remain one of the most important ways products are communicated. Whether customers are browsing an ecommerce site, searching a distributor catalog, or comparing products online, visuals often influence purchasing decisions before a single line of product data is read.

As digital commerce continues to grow, managing visual content has become just as important as creating it.

Manufacturers today manage far more than product images. They are responsible for videos, installation guides, lifestyle photography, logos, technical documents, 360 degree imagery, marketing materials, and more.

As product portfolios expand and content is needed across marketplaces, ecommerce platforms, and distribution partners, keeping those assets organized and accessible is becoming more difficult.

The challenge is no longer creating content. It’s managing it.

• Which image is the most current version?

• Has the latest logo been distributed everywhere?

• Are product photos consistent across partner websites?

• How do we get the right assets to customers and partners without creating more work?

Without a clear process, teams can spend more time looking for assets than actually using them.

One of the biggest challenges is maintaining consistency across channels.

An updated image may be available internally while an older version continues to appear on websites, distributor portals, catalogs, and marketing materials. The result can be inconsistent branding, outdated information, and confusion throughout the supply chain.

This is one reason companies are turning to centralized digital asset management systems that provide a single source of truth and make it easier to keep content current across multiple channels.

Digital Asset Management Solutions such as TecAlliance Pixey are helping companies address this challenge by giving them greater control over digital assets while reducing some of the manual work involved in keeping content current across teams and trading partners.

A single product image may need to be published in multiple sizes, formats, and resolutions depending on where it is being used.

Historically, teams have managed these variations manually, creating duplicate files and increasing the risk of errors. Today, systems can automatically generate different versions from a single master file, including resizing, format conversion, border application, and optimization.

Instead of maintaining dozens of versions of the same asset, teams can manage one source file and let the system handle many of the variations required for different channels.

As asset libraries grow, finding the right content becomes a challenge of its own.

Companies are relying more heavily on metadata to organize assets using product attributes, brands, vehicle applications, campaigns, and other business specific information. A well-structured metadata strategy can turn a digital asset library from simple storage into a searchable business resource.

For the aftermarket, where product relationships and application data can be complex, being able to find the right content is becoming just as important as storing it.

Managing and storing content is only part of the challenge. Manufacturers and suppliers also need to deliver that content to distributors, retailers, marketplaces, sales teams, marketers, and other partners, often in different formats and through different methods.

Digital asset management is therefore moving beyond storage and organization to include how content is shared and distributed throughout the supply chain.

Organizations using platforms such as Pixey can more effectively manage, distribute, and deliver the right content to the right people across the supply chain.

Visual content has always influenced how people understand products and make decisions. What’s changing is the scale and complexity of managing that content.

Across the aftermarket, companies are dealing with more products, more channels, more partners, and more digital content than ever before. Keeping assets synchronized, creating the right versions, making content easy to find, and getting it where it needs to go are becoming important parts of managing product information.

Ultimately, effective digital asset management is about making it easier to find the right content, keep it current, and get it where it needs to go, so businesses can spend less time managing content and more time using it.

On Sep. 6, General Motors notified dealers they will need to resolve an issue with a vacuum brake assist pump that makes it more difficult to engage the braking system and increases the risk for a crash. GM told CNN that the problem has resulted in 113 accidents  and 13 non-fatal injuries.

The problem appears to stem from excessive debris and sludge build-up on the vacuum pump filter screen as the engine oil lubricates it. This leads to a drop in vacuum and may necessitate more pressure applied to the brake pedal, create a “hard brake pedal,” and increase the time it takes to stop. Trucks and SUVs overdue for an oil change may be at a higher risk. Recalibrating the electronic brake control module to recognize lack of vacuum assist and activate hydraulic assist resolves the issue, GM says.

On the safety recall report, it’s noted that: “At all times, the brakes remain functional and exceed the requirements of S7.11 of Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS) No. 135, ‘Light Vehicle Brake Systems.’”

The NHTSA opened the investigation last November and the Office of Defects Investigation received 111 hard brake reports from the various affected trucks and SUVs. Nine of the vehicles were involved in low-speed collisions, where it looks like the issue is more prevalent. The ABS system supplies supplemental hydraulic brake assist if vacuum drops, though at a lower level under low speeds.

GM is responsible for notifying owners, but you can also visit https://www.nhtsa.gov/recalls and enter your VIN to see if your vehicle needs to be brought in and repaired. The NHTSA Safety Issue ID is 19V645000. The dealership will reprogram Electronic Brake Control Module to fix the problem.

The Jacobs compression release engine brake, or "Jake brake," is now in its 60th year of service, with more than 9 million of the systems manufactured by 2019. The   compression release brake   system, which turns the engine into an air compressor, has helped countless truckers slow down their truck by shifting stopping energy from the brakes and converting it into hot air released through the exhaust.

This has spared wear and tear on brakes the world over, extending their service life. More importantly, by reducing the friction on brakes during long downhill stretches, the Jake brake keeps them from failing when the trucker needs them most.

And it all started when the founding father of U.S. diesel engines nearly lost his life due to failing brakes and an inopportune train schedule.

Ninety years ago, Clessie Cummins, founder and namesake of the engine manufacturer, Cummins Inc. , along with two compatriots, hopped in a diesel truck specially outfitted with bunks, storage and stove for an incredulous journey across America to test the endurance of diesel trucks. That 3,214-mile trip from New York to California trailblazed the way for every long-hauler who followed, all for the fuel cost of $11.22, or $194.15 in today’s dollars. But it almost cost Cummins his life.

Dashing down the Cajon Pass on the old Route 66 in California, which has an apex of 3,777 ft. above sea level, Cummins saw a train roaring across the road below. As legend goes, he barely missed T-boning the caboose as the truck crossed the tracks. In the decades that followed, Cummins kept that near-miss — and how to avoid another — close to his heart.

“In the ’50s, when he finally retired from Cummins, he spent some time working on that and trying to figure out how to turn the engine into some sort of compressive brake,” explained Steve Ernest, vice president, Engineering and Business Development for Jacobs Vehicle Systems , the company that formed in 1961 to commercialize the braking innovation.

“As you’re going down along a hill, you get some push back from the engine on the truck. That way the foundation brakes are nice and cool and ready to go in the event you do have to do an emergency stop or really slow down very quickly,” Ernest explained.

This additional retardation helps slow the vehicle, reducing the friction on the foundation brakes. Ernest said the Jake Brake extends brake life by two to three times.

While Volvo uses its own compression brake, Jacobs has 100% penetration on Detroit Diesel and Cummins X15 engines and 92% on Navistar’s A26 engine. A study of International trucks found the $2,500 cost of the system is recouped upon resale.

Owner-operator Grant E. Sheldon found the Jake Brake saves him $1,000 per year in brake maintenance costs.

“I use the Jake Brake like crazy and because of that, I easily double the life of my foundation brakes,” said the Kentucky-based driver with 50 years of trucking experience.

Jacobs has continued to innovate with such solutions as Cylinder Deactivation Technology (CDA) , which can cut fuel consumption by 5% while reducing NOx emissions as well.

Though a decade ago it was far from the case, nowadays, the likelihood for a technician to work on a newer truck with air disc brakes (ADBs) is about the same as one with drum brakes.

“Almost half of the builds for new equipment are for disc brakes today,” noted Mark Holley, director of marketing and customer solutions for wheel ends at Bendix Commercial Vehicle Systems . “With new trailers, it’s about 20%.”

Both types can provide some value to fleets, and when evaluating whether a drum or disc brake is the better overall fit, fleets should consider the benefits relative to the application they will be placed in. The total cost of ownership, including the maintenance and service, also factors into a brake’s longer-term ROI.

To help you calculate which is more suitable for your duty cycles and assets, we talked to leading brake experts about how service is done on each and what to look out for.

ADBs and drums have a few things in common, of course. Primarily, they both arrest vehicle movement, which takes a toll each time it happens.

“Friction and rotors will wear, as will friction and drums,” said Kevin Pfost, wheel end product specialist at Bendix.

But to discern the amount of wear, technicians must go about this in different ways.

“Visually and with a tool, a technician can measure friction and drum thickness,” Pfost said. “With a disc brake, we have a tool to measure rotor thickness. A technician can also measure the percentage of friction. So comparatively, disc brakes and drum brakes are the same in terms of visual inspections.”

See also: Tips to safely survive Roadcheck 2023

The difference presents itself when the time comes to actually service the brakes.

Changing ADB pads takes roughly half the time of drum brakes, according to Joe Kay, director of engineering for Cummins-Meritor , a global power technology company whose products include disc and s-cam drum brakes.

Drum brakes not only require additional time but oftentimes more effort.

“With disc brakes, you don’t have to pull off a heavy drum in order to change the friction,” Pfost explained. “With disc brakes, you’re only pulling wheels off.”

Furthermore, with a drum brake system, the technician is nowhere near done after removing the drum. There are brake shoes to deal with, which Pfost said can be a challenge in their own right. After that, the cam head should be cleaned up and inspected for wear or damage.

See also: Biden visits Cummins amid OEM's $1B manufacturing investment

“You should really use a dial indicator to measure bushing wear on the cam head,” Pfost added. “If it’s out of spec, there is even more to do. You might have to pull the slack adjuster off, pull the cams and bushings out, and put new bushings back in. You might find that the clevis pin is seized into the slack adjuster. Now you have to spend time working that out. You don’t have to do any of this on a disc brake because everything is internal.”

To service a disc brake, the friction removal process simply involves a spring clip, pin, and pad-retaining bar. Then you just pull out the worn pads. Next, push the caliper all the way inward, inspect the guide pin boots to make sure they aren’t torn, ensure that the caliper can slide freely, and inspect the boots on the tappets (pistons) in the caliper. If everything checks out OK, clean the carrier, measure rotor thickness to ensure it is within spec, and drop the new pads in.

See also: Questions to ask after measuring maintenance data

“A technician can typically do all of that within 15 minutes per wheel end,” Pfost said, adding that a thorough drum brake inspection can push upwards of an hour.

“There will always be a technician who says they can change out brake shoes in 10 minutes,” Pfost continued. “They probably can, but they haven’t done any measuring. If a drum brake job isn’t done properly, you can run into problems like adjustment issues and hang-ups later in the brake’s life.”

There are also more moving parts with a drum brake. Plus, those parts are exposed to the elements, which increases the opportunities for contamination and damage.

“With a disc brake, you just have a caliper, rotor, and hub,” Pfost said.

One potential issue with a disc brake is if the rotor becomes damaged. Pfost said replacing a rotor is more time-consuming than replacing a drum. The caliper carrier assembly must be removed, followed by the hub and rotor. The standard repair time is around 100 minutes.

“Premature failures will always have an adverse impact to any ROI,” Pfost said. “But over the long-term, a rotor’s life expectancy is longer than that of a drum, helping reduce the total cost of ownership. Fleets could use our Bendix ADB Value Calculator (valuebybendix.com) to see the directional difference.”

According to Pfost, rotors are designed to last at least several hundred thousand miles in on-highway applications with properly scheduled maintenance.

“Inspection for premature pad and rotor wear and early detection of conditions such as cracking or discoloring are vital to ensuring the life of the rotor,” Pfost said. “Drums get changed with every friction/shoe replacement.”

He added genuine Bendix pads and rotors can provide “at least two or three pad lives per rotor.”

If there’s one thing on commercial vehicles that operations and maintenance professionals need to understand, it’s braking systems. Not getting a truck to start rolling on time will cause delayed deliveries and missed work. Not getting it to stop will cause all that and a whole lot more, including property damage, injuries, and even death. Improper brake maintenance also will leave fleets and shops vulnerable to “nuclear” verdicts .

The good news is that fleets that keep up to date with the latest braking technology, as well as related preventive maintenance and inspections, shouldn’t lose any sleep over brake issues.

As a key element of safety, commercial vehicle stopping distances are codified in law. Specifically, FMVSS (Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard) 121 calls for air brake systems to fully stop tractor-trailers in no more than 250 ft. when loaded to their gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR) at 60 mph. This is true for commercial vehicles using either air disc brakes or S-cam drum brakes.

So, which type of brake can better help you meet these FMVSS standards?

According to Bendix Commercial Vehicle Systems , a 6x4 tractor-trailer going 60 mph takes 200 ft. to stop with air disc brakes and 225 ft. with drum brakes. An independent test of Bendix ADB22X air disc brakes completed on a test track by Pitt Ohio revealed that at 55 mph, these ADBs stopped 15 ft. earlier than drums.

“Fifteen feet is the length of a car,” noted Jeff Mercadante, VP of safety at Pitt Ohio , a perennial fleet safety award winner. “When you get up to 70 mph, you’re talking closer to 50 to 60 ft.”

Drum brakes, though, make up the majority of systems in trucking, as they initially cost less. ADBs, however, have gained market share in the last decade. In 2015, ADB adoption was about 15%, while in 2020 it doubled to 30%. ADBs have fewer parts for quicker servicing, which can lead to higher uptime and a better total cost of ownership. But that hardly settles the debate.

Terrance Wall, senior manager of maintenance technical support at Ryder , pointed out that for decades, S-cam type drum brake systems have been the “go-to” standard for medium- and heavy-duty trucks and tractors.

“Drum brakes are a consistent economical solution that provides common components across multiple vehicle platforms as well as weight classes,” he said. “And since the implementation of reduced stopping distance regulations in 2013, drum brake lining manufacturers have improved materials to meet or exceed the stopping distance requirements.”

“Although air disc brakes do have a slightly shorter stopping distance, drum brakes still easily meet the requirements,” Wall continued. “Air disc brake systems do have an advantage when brakes heat up and brake fade becomes more evident, but with a multi-vocational fleet, a uniform and economical option becomes the primary focus second only to safety.”

For Ryder, that is where drum brake systems have an advantage. When operating a wide variety of vehicles and with multiple repair locations, standard practices that include uniform training, tooling, and maintenance procedures are paramount to maximizing the useful life of brake components while maintaining the safety and cost effectiveness of the brake system.

Penske Truck Leasing , meanwhile, mostly specs ADBs. “To capitalize on their full benefit, however, both the tractor and trailer need to be equipped with air disc brakes,” noted Chris Hough, Penske’s VP of maintenance, design, and engineering.

Air disc brakes benefit the Penske fleet in several ways. In the area of safety, Hough noted, they provide shorter stopping distances and reduced brake fade. From a maintenance standpoint, there are fewer moving parts and grease points, and no need to measure brake stroke. Also, pad replacements are a relatively quick and simple process. Penske shops also are stocked with brake vendor-specific tools, along with hub handlers and various gauges to measure the remaining brake pad life and to inspect the rotor condition.

Hough also pointed out that ADBs have helped reduce the number of units placed out of service for brake stroke compliance issues during roadside inspections. “When it comes to ROI, there are some segments that are hard to measure,” he explained. “In general, we have found that ADBs provide a lower brake maintenance [cost per mile], provide our customers with improved stopping distances, and increase uptime.”

The advent of new technologies such as lane departure, electronic stability, and adaptive cruise control, which are now being integrated with ABS systems, also contribute a great deal to extending the life of foundation brake systems, he added. ADB systems also offer electronic pad wear sensors, which can provide data via telematics to assist in PM interval planning and procedures.

“All brake component manufacturers provide specific maintenance procedures to ensure optimal performance and life from these components,” Hough said. “By integrating these procedures into your brake maintenance program, coupled with the utilization of the correct tools, the maximum useful life at the most economical cost can be realized.”

“ADB systems provide benefits such as less time required to replace lining material and fewer components to lubricate,” Hough continued. “However, even with these benefits, ADB systems typically cost more to maintain and are difficult to standardize across a multi-vocational fleet without maintaining a larger inventory to accommodate the different spec and lining requirements.”

Another year, another chance for the trucking industry to focus on brake safety. Let’s go over what fleets and drivers need to know for this year’s Brake Safety Week.

According to the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance , Brake Safety Week is a commercial motor vehicle and driver inspection and regulatory compliance enforcement initiative, a brake-safety awareness and outreach opportunity, and a brake-related inspection and violation data collection project. Each year, this event is hosted by CVSA.

This means that inspections will be conducted throughout Brake Safety Week with particular focus on brake performance. Vehicles can be taken out of service if brake violations are discovered.

Brake Safety Week this year will be August 25-31. According to past CVSA records, Brake Safety Week typically occurs at the end of August.

Unlike Brake Safety Day , another CVSA event—the date of which goes unannounced until after the event has occurred—fleets have time and the knowledge needed to prepare for Brake Safety Week.

How should fleets prepare for Brake Safety Week?

The emphasis of Brake Safety Week this year will be on the condition of brake linings and pads. Inspectors will be looking for excessive wear in the brake linings and pads, particularly cracks, according to Jim Ward, senior safety manager at Transervice Logistics .

Ward said that one red flag that drivers may not think twice about but inspectors will is rubbing air lines.

“Those [rubbing air lines] get written up a lot,” Ward said. “If you have two brake lines—which some of them are rubber, others are like a poly material—what happens is those two hoses have a lot of pressure going through them, and they're sitting right next to each other. So over time, with the vibration of the truck, they tend to rub against each other, and they can start leaving little marks on each other. Sometimes they'll wear down far enough to actually put a big chafe into the hose. To me, that's something that's overlooked. It may look fine, but if those two hoses are touching, you're going to get written up for it because you should make sure that they’re kept separated.”

See also: CVSA releases results of 2024 Brake Safety Day

To prepare for Brake Safety Week, Ward suggests focusing on pre- and post-trip inspections as well as preventive maintenance .

“The most important thing is PM and pre-trip inspections,” Ward said. “Make sure that the trucks are PM’d on a regular basis … When you're a driver, the most important thing for you to continue to do is pre-trip. Pre-trip inspect your vehicle because it saves your life and the people in front of you or people around you.”

What will the results of Brake Safety Week be?

According to CVSA, Brake Safety Week in 2022 resulted in 13.3% out-of-service violations. This decreased to 12.6% in 2023. This trend may continue in 2024, however, it’s also possible that safety technology will result in more accurate brake performance inspections.

This year, CVSA announced that performance-based brake testers (PBBTs) will be used in some jurisdictions during Brake Safety Week. PBBTs are machines that test brake performance. They measure the slow-speed brake force and weight at each wheel of a vehicle, add up the total vehicle brake force, and divide it by the total vehicle weight to determine overall vehicle braking efficiency.

It’s difficult to speculate, but the use of this technology could affect the percentage of out-of-service violations with more accurate measurements of brake performance.

According to CVSA, brake violations comprise the largest percentage of out-of-service violations cited during roadside inspections. CVSA cites that in last year’s International Roadcheck , brake violations were the top vehicle violation, comprising 25.2% of all vehicle out-of-service violations during those three days.

Brake Safety Week serves as a reminder to drivers and fleet managers of the importance of vehicle maintenance and provides an opportunity for law enforcement to highlight the importance of brake safety for all.

Most of those differences have involved components under the hood or in the exhaust system. Euro 7 changes that pattern by placing brake and tire wear under regulatory scrutiny.

These requirements will not change how you service vehicles next week. However, they have the potential to influence brake-system designs, friction materials, rotor construction, replacement tires and the types of vehicles entering your shop over the next decade.

Previous European emissions standards created service opportunities involving oxygen sensors, diesel particulate filters, selective catalytic reduction systems and other components. Euro 7’s brake and tire provisions could have the opposite effect by extending some replacement intervals. At the same time, they could make selecting and installing the correct replacement components more important—and potentially more expensive.

Internal-combustion engines now operate at historically low levels of particulate matter and other regulated pollutants. Battery-electric vehicles produce no tailpipe emissions, but they still generate particles from their brakes and tires. As exhaust emissions decline, these non-exhaust sources represent a larger portion of the particles attributed to road transportation.

European Union Regulation 2024/1257, commonly known as Euro 7, introduces limits on brake-particle emissions from passenger cars and light commercial vehicles for the first time.

Beginning November 29, 2026, newly approved passenger-car and light-commercial-vehicle types must comply with Euro 7.

The initial brake-emission limit for most passenger vehicles is 7 milligrams per kilometer. The limit for battery-electric passenger vehicles is 3 milligrams per kilometer. These limits apply to PM10—the mass of airborne particles with an aerodynamic diameter of 10 microns or smaller.

Brake emissions are measured according to procedures based on United Nations Global Technical Regulation No. 24. A complete brake corner is operated on an inertia dynamometer inside a controlled enclosure. The brake is subjected to a standardized cycle intended to represent urban, rural and highway operation. Instruments collect and measure the particles released during the test.

The regulation distinguishes among powertrain configurations and accounts for the amount of braking performed by the friction brakes. That gives electrified vehicles an advantage because regenerative braking converts vehicle motion into electrical energy rather than heat and wear at the pads and rotors.

The important distinction is that Euro 7 measures airborne wear material. It is not a stopping-distance, pedal-feel or friction-equivalency standard. A replacement pad might comply with a traditional performance requirement such as UN Regulation No. 90 and still require separate evaluation for brake-particle emissions.

Producing friction between a brake pad and rotor inevitably removes some material. The amount released depends on the friction formulation, rotor metallurgy, surface treatment, temperature, pressure and how the two components interact.

A pad with a low wear rate does not automatically produce low emissions. Material removed from the pad or rotor can remain attached to the components, fall to the road as larger debris or become suspended in the air as fine particles. Consequently, manufacturers must evaluate the pad and rotor as a system.

European manufacturers and brake suppliers are pursuing several solutions. One is the development of new friction formulations designed to reduce wear without sacrificing stopping performance, temperature stability, noise control or pedal feel.

Another solution is a more wear-resistant rotor surface. Manufacturers are experimenting with hard-metal coatings, laser-applied coatings and other surface treatments that can reduce both rotor wear and corrosion. Some vehicles already use coated rotors, particularly on electrified applications where regenerative braking can leave the friction brakes unused for extended periods.

Installing a low-cost pad against an expensive coated rotor—or replacing a coated rotor with a conventional casting—could alter noise, wear, pedal feel and particle emissions. Matching the pad and rotor may become more important than selecting either component separately.

Longer pad and rotor life could reduce the frequency of conventional brake jobs. However, that does not mean electrified vehicles will be maintenance-free. Reduced friction-brake use can promote rotor corrosion, uneven contact patterns, sticking pads and seized caliper hardware. Shops may perform fewer wear-related brake jobs but more services involving corrosion, electronic parking brakes, brake-by-wire systems and preventive cleaning and lubrication.

Despite its age, the 2004-2013 Mazda 3 is a popular car you may very well see come through the shop —especially those on the tail end of that year range. Let’s go over the step-by-step brake job process.

- Understanding Brake Pad Wear Sensors for Imports

The 2004-2013 Mazda 3 is based on the Ford global C1 platform, shared with the European Ford Focus and Volvo S40. Nothing is really groundbreaking about the mechanical brake system, but not paying attention to the details can end in a post-brake-job comeback.

A key service issue concerns the hydraulics and ABS system. The older the car, the greater the chance the brake fluid has not been serviced. Over time this can cause issues with the ABS hydraulic control unit.

For almost 10 years, Mazda used the same caliper, pad and rotor design. Pads should be replaced when there is 2mm or less of friction material. If the rotors are any thicker, they have enough material on them to last at least one turning on the lathe. The runout specification for these vehicles is .002” and disc thickness variation should be far below .0005”.

Mazda claims repeated panic braking may raise the temperature in some portions of the disc plate by approx. 1,000°C (l,832°F). This temperature is almost near impossible to achieve this side of a high-speed police chase.

The calipers mount to the brackets using caliper guide pins with Allen heads. The sleeves and boots should be disassembled, cleaned and lubricated every time the brakes are replaced. The torque for the guide pins is 21 ft./lbs. and the caliper bracket bolts should be tightened to 75 ft./lbs.

All Mazda3 models have rear disc brakes. The calipers mount to the brackets using caliper guide pins with Allen heads. The sleeves and boots should be disassembled, cleaned and lubricated every time the brakes are replaced. The torque for the guide pins is 21 ft./lbs. and the caliper bracket bolts should be tightened to 55 ft./lbs.

Mazda uses a hand brake that is incorporated into the rear caliper, and a couple of systems are employed to retract rear pistons. The later-model cars require the familiar method of turning the piston clockwise while applying pressure, where others will have a plug on the back side of the caliper that provides access for an Allen wrench to facilitate retracting the piston. Be careful as you retract the piston.

After the pads are replaced, pump the pedal and adjust the parking brake mechanism in the rear calipers. If the level has too much travel, perform the following steps:

Remove the service hole cover of the rear console.

Turn the adjusting nut and adjust the parking brake lever.

After adjustment, pull the parking brake lever one notch and verify that the parking brake warning light illuminates and the rear brakes do not drag.

The Mazda3 comes in two styles, ABS and ABS with Dynamic Stability Control (DSC). Both systems connect to other vehicle components via a high-speed serial data bus. The DSC system ties more components together (like a yaw/pitch sensor and steering position sensor) onto the bus.

If you are seeing communication-related DTCs, it is essential that you fully diagnose problems with the system before you start replacing sensors and modules. Some of these vehicles have been on the road for more than six years and the connections will be starting to corrode and fret.

One of the main facilitators of ABS/DCS problems are the connectors, especially under the hood where the control/modulator unit connects. Being able to measure values at the connectors and observe data on a scan tool is essential for diagnosing problems.

The biggest ABS issue with the three generations of Mazda 3 is power. With some higher mileage vehicles, the battery cables, wiring from the power distribution box or the ground connection (behind the driver’s side headlight at G02) can have enough resistance so the voltage drops below 8 volts. When this happens, the ABS module cuts control and the electronic brake distribution system is disabled.

If a modulator/control unit is replaced, the pressure sensors must be recalibrated with a scan tool that is able to communicate with the chassis/ABS module. If this is not performed, it can result in brake failure and lock up.

If you have DTCs C1141, C1142, C1143, C1144, C1233, C1234, C1235 or C1236 (ABS wheel-speed sensor/ABS sensor rotor), chances are something is wrong with the wheel bearings. Another cause for these codes could be an accumulation of metal debris on the sensor. The front bearings are press-in cartridge-style units. Rear wheel bearings are hub units. In the front, the tone ring, or encoder, is on the inner seal of the bearing and the sensor is mounted in the knuckle. The parameters for these codes to be set include abnormalities in the signal such as a weak signal or large differences in the value when compared to the other sensors.

If you have DTCs C1145, C1155, C1165 or C1175 (open sensor), it could be damaged wiring or a failed sensor that is the problem. If you have more than one, chances are there is a problem with the connection at the control unit or in the front or rear harnesses of the sensors.

These DTCs will usually clear themselves after repairs are made and the vehicle is driven above 6.2 mph when the self-diagnostic check is performed.

Some customers may report a slight clunk, bang or jolt from the front of the vehicle. This concern will most likely occur during the vehicle’s first forward movement and after the vehicle sits for a few hours and/or a cold soak. This is a normal operating noise of the ABS system.

If you encounter a customer complaint for this concern, explain that the noise comes from the ABS/TCS/DSC “Malfunction Detection Function” initial check. The initial check is a necessary function to ensure the normal operation of the ABS/TCS/DSC system. This initial test function occurs during the vehicle’s first forward movement and when the vehicle reaches approximately 6.2 mph.

At one time, brake pad wear sensors were a pretty simple matter: the sensor was just a spring steel tab that was mounted on the backing plate and bent at a right angle. The tab was as long as the minimum depth for the pad’s friction material, so when the pad wore down to that minimum depth the tab would drag on the brake rotor and cause an unmistakable metal-on-metal screech that would alert the driver that it was time for new brakes. Unfortunately, many drivers don’t even know what that screech means or may not notice it in a vehicle that’s got a lot of sound deadening, and by the time they bring their car into the shop the rotors are already chewed up (and the vehicle is very unsafe to drive).

While many brake pads, both OEM and aftermarket, still feature these simple wear indicators, newer systems are more sophisticated. That means giving a driver a heads-up long before the pads get down to minimum thickness and start damaging the rotors through metal-to-metal contact.

Older brake pad wear sensors consisted of a loop of wire embedded in the friction material at a certain depth, with a low amount of current running through it  and the sensor looped into the vehicle’s ABS circuit and processor. This sensor had a known resistance value; when resistance would be above 2000 ohms, a rectifier circuit would read that as an open circuit and would light up an indicator on the dash. These designs could be prone to corrosion or physical damage (sometimes just due to heat from the brakes), and it was always recommended that the sensor be replaced along with the pads when it was time for a brake job.

Newer sensor designs are capable of actually giving a driver an estimate of the number of miles that are left on the pads. The key difference is that they’re designed with two resistor circuits in parallel with each other. The first circuit is set at a higher position in the sensor, with the second in a lower position. When the first circuit is broken, the parallel design means that the resistance will increase. If the second wire is broken, the circuit is then read as open, triggering the warning light on the dash.

With these two-stage sensor systems, the first circuit usually won’t trigger a warning light. Instead, the system starts to calculate remaining pad life with information about wheel rotational speed, mileage, brake pressure, brake rotor and pad temperature and total brake operating time. Splicing wires together to bypass the sensor won’t work – the module confirms the sensor is working by  passing voltage through the circuit. Splicing wires together would mean the system would read it as an open circuit and would set the dash warning light.

Most vehicles will have one sensor for the front axle and one for the rear, although some might be equipped with a sensor for each wheel. Some systems are designed for two-stage warnings, sometimes with a yellow indicator light for the first stage and a red light for when brake pad replacement is imminent.

Considering that the wire loop is destroyed as part of normal wear, it’s necessary to replace the sensor when doing a brake job. Even if the customer gets the vehicle in early and the sensors haven’t been triggered, the old sensors will already be partially worn and could have damaged leads. Be sure you’re using the proper sensors for the vehicle’s year/make/model, as different sensors have different lead lengths, connector types and mounting designs.

For Mercedes-Benz, Audi, Volkswagen, Mini and BMW models, it’s necessary to perform a reset after replacing the pads and sensors.

While the process can vary from one year/make/model to another, a typical reset might involve these steps:

Turn on the ignition by pressing the start/stop button once or twice without your foot on the brake pedal (don’t start the engine).

Wait for all the dashboard lights and chimes to finish.

Find the BC button on the turn signal stalk to cycle through until it displays time and mileage/trip odometer.

Press and hold the odometer reset button until you see a service menu on the instrument cluster.

Use the stalk button to scroll through the options until you see the Brake Pad Service icon.

Press and hold the button again until “Reset?” appears.

Release the button quickly, then press and hold again until the reset occurs and the mileage counter is updated.

For BMW models, this may have to be done through the vehicle’s iDrive system.

Installation is usually a pretty simple affair. Locate the wire that runs from the brake pad to the wheel well housing or junction box, and undo any fender liner clips or protective access doors. Unplug the sensor by pushing the plastic release tab on its connector. If there are any guide clips along the brake line, carefully unclip them. The sensor can then be pulled or pried from its slot on the interior brake pad. Installation is the reverse of removal, as you push the new sensor head firmly into the slot on the pad and route the wire along the exact same path as before. Be sure to reinstall any clips, rubber grommets or brackets.

Brake pad replacement on a T1XX Silverado or Sierra is tied into more systems than the friction material alone. These trucks use an electric brake pad life monitor, axle-specific wear sensors and an electric parking brake at the rear. The brake master cylinder can also pressurize the hydraulic system during an automated self-test. A routine pad job therefore requires a controlled shutdown, correct sensor handling and the proper reset or calibration before the truck leaves the bay.

- Modern Maintenance Requires More Than Checking Mileage

- When the Alignment is Green, But the Steering Isn’t Right

Here’s one critical safety step: Disconnect the negative battery cable before caliper service so an automated self-test cannot pressurize the master cylinder when a door is opened or the key transmitter wakes the vehicle.

For rear brake work, place the parking brake in Parking Brake Service Mode before disconnecting the battery. Then raise and support the truck using the approved lift points and remove the wheel. Observe normal brake-dust and brake-fluid precautions, and keep fluid off painted surfaces. If a hose is opened, plug both sides immediately to limit fluid loss and contamination. Use new sealing washers during assembly, bleed the hydraulic system, inspect for leaks and restore the reservoir with GM-approved fluid from a clean, sealed container.

The Driver Information Center normally displays front and rear pad life as a percentage. Near the calculated end of pad life, the message changes to an estimated distance remaining and repeats at ignition cycles so the driver can schedule service. If the system detects a supply-voltage fault, it can label the value invalid.

The Brake System Control Module has one input for the front axle sensor and one for the rear. It supplies voltage to each sensor; the sensors use vehicle ground. Inside each sensor are breakable wire resistors. The module combines that signal with its wear algorithm to calculate the displayed percentage. It is an estimate, so the technician still needs to inspect both sides of each axle. After pads are replaced, perform the Axle Brake Pad Life Monitor Reset Learn..

Rear Caliper and Electronic Parking Brake

The left-rear caliper carries the rear wear sensor. After entering Parking Brake Service Mode and disconnecting the battery, remove the bleeder-valve cap to free the sensor routing, disconnect the electrical connector and remove the sensor from the pad. Replace the rear pads if the sensor has contacted the rotor. Handle the replacement head carefully, reconnect it, reinstall the bleeder cap and reset the brake pad life monitor after the truck is lowered.

For complete rear caliper service, disconnect the parking-brake actuator connector. Remove the two actuator bolts, lift off the actuator and discard the actuator-lever seal. If the hydraulic hose is disconnected, discard both sealing washers and plug the hose. Remove the two guide-pin bolts and the caliper. Support the caliper whenever the hose remains attached; never hang it by the hose.

During assembly, tighten the rear guide-pin bolts to specification, use new hose washers and install a new parking-brake actuator-lever seal. Re-fit the actuator, tighten its bolts to the current VIN-specific specification and reconnect its electrical connector. After reconnecting the battery, bleed and leak-check any opened hydraulic circuit.

The final step after lowering the truck is Park Brake Calibration. Service Mode and calibration are separate steps: Service Mode prepares the mechanism for work; calibration restores correct operation after service.

Verify wheel, brake-hose fitting and parking-brake actuator fastener values in the current VIN-specific service information; those values were not included in the supplied quick-reference sheet.

Rapid rear pad wear – Bulletin 21-NA-089 , dated Oct. 30, 2024, covers 2019-2025 Silverado and Sierra 1500 configurations identified in the bulletin, generally those without RPO RG1. Dirt, mud or debris can pack into the rear calipers and hold the pads against the rotors. When mud is confirmed as the cause, GM calls for shielded calipers with dirt deflectors. The RG1 shielded caliper became a dealer-installed option for 2021, and the bulletin specifically says it can be installed on 2019-2021 light-duty 1500 pickups not built with the option. Current listed parts are 85140318 left and 85140319 right.

Excessive brake dust – Bulletin 18-NA-067 , revised May 6, 2024, describes black dust as a normal result of the high-performance pad material, made more visible by large wheel openings. GM recommends a soft cloth, mild soap and water, followed by a clean-water rinse and soft-towel drying. Strong chemicals, acids, abrasive cleaners and abrasive brushes can damage aluminum or chrome wheels and caliper finishes. Do not direct a power washer at the caliper, because it may remove copper paste from the pads and require the lubricant to be reapplied.

Before release, verify sensor and hose routing, connector engagement, pad-retaining hardware, fluid level and pedal feel. Reset the correct axle’s pad life monitor, perform Park Brake Calibration when the rear actuator or caliper has been serviced, clear related faults and road-test the truck. On these pickups, the friction work is only complete when the electronic monitoring and parking-brake functions are complete too.

Imagine being a belt on the front of the engine. Yours is a balancing act that is always being upset by change from the inputs from the crank pulley and the loads from the alternator, AC compressor and maybe a power steering pump. Your mission is to keep in contact with the grooves on the pulleys. You can’t hold on too tightly, because it could decrease fuel economy and damage the bearings inside the water pump, idler bushings and other components. But you can’t be too loose because it will cause you to slip, resulting in wear and noise.

A serpentine belt transfers torque through friction between its ribs and the pulley grooves. The belt must be held tightly enough against the pulleys to prevent slipping under the system’s maximum expected expected load.

As mentioned before, if tension is too low, the belt can microslip or visibly slip. This generates heat, polishes the belt ribs and pulley grooves, and may produce a chirp or squeal. Slippage can also reduce alternator output, power steering assist, coolant-pump speed or AC compressor performance.

Excessive tension creates a different set of problems. Every accessory shaft experiences a radial load from the belt. Raising belt tension increases that load, which can accelerate bearing wear in the alternator, water pump, idlers, tensioner and AC compressor. It also increases belt fatigue as the belt repeatedly bends around the pulleys. The additional bearing friction and belt deformation represent a small but measurable parasitic loss.

The correct tension is consequently the lowest tension that can reliably transmit the required torque under all operating conditions. That reduces friction and improves efficiency while preserving traction and controlling noise.

An automatic tensioner’s spring applies the required static tension, while an internal damping mechanism controls rapid arm movement. The damping prevents the tensioner from bouncing in response to engine firing pulses and accessory-load changes. Insufficient tension causes slippage, heat and noise, while excessive tension contributes to accessory wear. Some belt companies tensioner guidance also identifies excessive arm oscillation as a sign of a failed damping system or another drive-system problem.

What Happens When Accessory Load Increases?

The belt does not have identical tension everywhere around its path. When the crankshaft is driving an accessory, the belt span pulling the accessory pulley becomes the tight side. The belt leaving that pulley has less tension. The difference between those forces, combined with pulley radius, produces the torque that turns the accessory.

When alternator electrical output increases, electromagnetic resistance inside the alternator rises. The crankshaft must supply more torque through the belt. The tension difference across the alternator pulley increases, and the belt may elongate elastically by a very small amount. The tensioner moves to manage that change.

A hydraulic power steering pump produces a similar reaction when the driver turns the steering wheel, especially near the steering stop. Pump pressure and required input torque rise rapidly. On systems with belt-driven AC compressors, compressor engagement can create an even sharper load change.

These loads are why a belt drive may operate quietly in the bay but squeal when the headlights, blower motor and rear defroster are switched on, when the steering wheel is turned at idle or when the AC compressor engages. The added load exposes marginal tension, worn ribs, pulley contamination or misalignment.

Technicians should reproduce the operating condition instead of judging the drive only at unloaded idle.

Engine-Speed Changes and Tension Reversals

Crankshaft speed is not perfectly constant. Each combustion event accelerates the crankshaft, while compression strokes and drivetrain events slow it. Those variations become more pronounced during startup, shutdown, throttle changes, transmission shifts and cylinder-deactivation transitions.

During acceleration, the belt must accelerate the rotating mass of every accessory. The alternator is particularly important because its rotor normally turns several times faster than the crankshaft. Its inertia resists a sudden increase in belt speed.

During rapid engine deceleration, the situation changes. The alternator rotor wants to continue spinning and can momentarily drive against the decelerating belt. The normal tight- and slack-side relationship does not permanently swap during ordinary operation, because the crankshaft remains the primary power source. However, local belt forces can equalize or briefly reverse during a transient event. The tensioner arm may then move sharply as the tension disturbance travels through the drive.

This can produce intermittent chirps, belt slap or tensioner rattle that does not occur at steady engine speed. A noise heard only during startup, shutdown, throttle tip-in or a downshift is therefore an important diagnostic clue.

Many late-model applications use an overrunning alternator pulley or overrunning alternator decoupler  (OAD) to control these events. The pulley allows the alternator to overrun the belt during rapid deceleration. An OAD also uses an internal torsion spring to absorb speed and tension fluctuations. This arrangement reduces vibration and allows the alternator to freewheel during deceleration.

A seized decoupler can act like a solid pulley, causing excessive tensioner movement and a chirp during startup or shutdown. Installing a solid pulley where an OAD was specified can create noise and shorten belt and tensioner life.

According to Mobility Global ’s latest forecast, U.S. light-vehicle sales are expected to reach 16.1 million units in 2026 and 16.4 million by the end of the decade, remaining below the roughly 17 million annual sales levels that defined the market before the pandemic. Analysts speaking at a Mobility Global media briefing said affordability remains the single biggest challenge facing consumers, contributing to a fundamentally different market environment.

The discussion came at a pivotal moment for the industry. Automakers are navigating geopolitical instability, economic uncertainty, and shifting trade policies, even as consumers wrestle with the persistent problem of what they can afford.

Affordability Pressures Curb Recovery to Pre-Pandemic Volumes

The U.S. automotive market has remained depressed since the pandemic, with some of that due to supply chain shortages. But right now, the main reason Mobility Global doesn’t see the market returning to those previous levels and remaining below its potential is the affordability issue.

“We don’t see the U.S. returning to pre-pandemic levels of volumes,” said Peter Nagle, associate director for Americas demand forecasting. “Obviously, there is something constraining the market from those 17-million-unit thresholds that we routinely hit back in, say, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019.”

Policy Shifts Reshape Product Plans and Powertrain Mix

A myriad of factors have reshaped the automotive landscape in recent years. The past year has brought some significant changes to the U.S. regulatory and incentive framework — and in the compressed span of automotive timeframes. As emissions and fuel economy rules loosened, automakers rewrote product plans almost overnight.

“The resulting wave of battery-electric vehicle (BEV) cancellations may leave some suppliers wary of chasing future BEV programs,” said Eric Anderson, associate director for light vehicle powertrain forecasting. Even so, Mobility Global expects BEV assembly in North America to once again surpass 1 million units in 2027, according to its latest forecast.

The internal combustion engine vehicles and hybrids, however, the analysts said, are expected to remain central to the market as consumers continue to weigh cost, convenience and lifestyle in choosing their next car. Mobility Global forecasts North American assembly of full hybrid electric vehicles (FHEVs) to surpass 3 million units in 2027 — a 25% annual increase — with nearly a third of all North American light-vehicle assembly expected to be FHEV by 2030.

Regionalization Accelerates as China Shapes Global Strategies

The briefing also turned to China’s growing influence on the global automotive landscape. Analysts explored how conditions in China’s domestic market could shape automaker strategies worldwide. They pointed to a broader industry move toward regionalization and de-globalization.

“The auto industry is moving toward three major regional islands,” said Joe Langley, director of research and analysis. “North America, Europe and Asia, and automakers will increasingly have to build where they sell and design for the regions they serve. The difficult part is doing that while costs continue to rise.”

And there is no longer one global recipe for success, Langley added.
